title: Edmonton and Montreal battle for the last Grey Cup of this era
summary: CBC Sports' daily newsletter previews the 113th Grey Cup game, which is the final one before the CFL introduces some controversial new rules and an expanded playoffs next year.

image.caption: CFL Most Outstanding Player Davis Alexander will lead a high-powered Montreal Alouettes offence against a stout Edmonton Elks defence in the Grey Cup. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: CBC Sports' daily newsletter previews the 113th Grey Cup game, which is the final one before the CFL introduces some controversial new rules and an expanded playoffs next year.
CFL's top two teams square off for the title before new rules arrive

One of the great traditions in Canadian sports continues on Sunday in Calgary as the Edmonton Elks and the Montreal Alouettes square off in the 113th Grey Cup. This is Montreal's third appearance in the CFL title game in four years (they won in 2023 and lost last year to Saskatchewan) while Edmonton returns for the first time since winning the Cup in 2015.

The Elks missed the playoffs in each of the past five seasons and endured a 22-game home losing streak that stretched nearly four full years before they snapped it in August 2023 (the cancellation of the 2020 season due to the COVID pandemic helped lengthen the time frame). They improved from 7-11 the last two years to a West Division-leading 13-5 with an old-school formula: run the ball, play strong defence, and win the turnover battle.

Edmonton's D did its part by allowing the fewest points and yards in the CFL while leading the league in interceptions and fumbles forced. On offence, the Elks topped the league in rushing yards with a strong running-back duo of Justin Rankin and ShunDerrick Powell and duel-threat quarterback Cody Fajardo leading the charge. The 34-year-old Fajardo threw for a career-high 4,788 yards and 25 touchdowns with an acceptable 10 picks while topping all QBs with 517 rushing yards before adding another 84 yards on the ground in last week's 28-16 playoff win over B.C.

However, sometimes the best defence is a good offence. And Montreal, which led the league in total yards gained, is favoured by a field goal this Sunday on the strength of a dynamite passing attack featuring some explosive stars.

Quarterback Davis Alexander, who was hampered by a bad hamstring in last year's Grey Cup loss, powered the Alouettes to a league-best 14-4 record and captured the CFL's Most Outstanding Player award after ranking second in the league in both passing yards and touchdowns (35) while throwing just four interceptions. He remained on top of his game in last week's 33-23 victory over Winnipeg in the East final, throwing for 372 yards and a pair of TDs.

Montreal also has an incredibly dynamic duo of receivers in Tyson Philpot and Tyler Snead, who ranked No. 1 and 2 in the league in receiving yards and each caught 13 TDs this season. Philpot, especially dangerous after he catches the ball, was named the CFL's Most Outstanding Canadian before piling up a game-high 129 yards on nine grabs in the playoff win against Winnipeg. And, just in case Edmonton didn't have enough to worry about, depth receiver Charleston Rambo went off for 117 yards on three catches against the Blue Bombers.

This interesting matchup between the two best teams in the league should make for a good send-off in the final Grey Cup before second-year commissioner Stewart Johnston's most controversial rules changes take effect. Starting next year, the length of the field will be reduced from the CFL-signature 110 yards to the NFL standard of 100. The endzones are also shrinking, from 20 yards to 15, while the goalposts move from the goal line to the back of the endzone. The objective of all these reforms is, in Johnston's words, "trading field goals for touchdowns."

Big changes are also coming to the playoff format as eight of the league's nine teams will qualify (up from six currently) and there will be three rounds before the Grey Cup instead of two. The revamped first round even includes a pair of non-elimination games among the top two seeds in each division, who will square off for a bye to the semifinals. You can see the goal here: creating more inventory to sell to playoff-hungry broadcast partners, whose annual bill for rights fees is increasing from $50 million to about $83 million next year.

Johnston spoke on another hot topic today during his annual state of the league address, confirming that Quebec City has emerged as a leading candidate for the CFL's long-sought 10th franchise. He said the league is talking to a prospective owner but declined to give more details.

Earlier today, the CFL and the players' union announced that they've agreed to participate in a training camp for those interested in representing Canada in flag football at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. It will take place from Nov. 29 to Dec. 5 in the San Diego area and 20 CFL players were invited. They include the Alouettes' Tyson Philpot and B.C. quarterback Nathan Rourke, who won the Most Outstanding Player award last year. According to the CFL, the players will "learn the rules, techniques, concepts and schemes of the international flag football game, under the guidance and evaluation of Team Canada coaches."

Flag football will make its Olympic debut at the L.A. Games, and Canada earned a spot in the men's tournament by winning the bronze-medal game at the world championships in Germany in August. The Canadian women's team also qualified before upsetting the United States to win gold.

While the CFL and its nine teams have "agreed to the parameters" of making their players available for the Olympics, it's unclear how the Canadian roster will be picked. Current members of the national team have a strong claim to be on it after their success at the worlds, and the NFL has also expressed its support for the Olympics, which could open the door for Canadian standouts like running backs Chase Brown and Chuba Hubbard to take part.
